lessons.title: Values, assignment, and decisions
lessons.objective: Trace typed values and sequential assignments, evaluate arithmetic and Boolean conditions, and select the correct branch including equality boundaries.
scope: Python 3 integers, floats, strings and Boolean values; input text requires explicit conversion
Assignment evaluates the old right side before rebinding; distinguish = from ==
Arithmetic precedence, ** exponent, / true division, // floor division and % with positive divisor, including negatives
if/elif/else executes first true branch; and/or/not and boundary conditions
workedExamples: Trace x=4; y=x+2; x=y*3
Distinguish '12' from 12 and int('12')
Parenthesized arithmetic and exponent vs XOR
Trace threshold decisions below/at/above 10
Compare if/elif with two separate if statements
Combine an inclusive range with and rather than or
Short circuit prevents division by zero

interaction.purpose: Choose an input and threshold, predict assigned values and the branch, then advance a numbered state trace one step at a time. Change an equality boundary and explain the result.

mistakes: Treat assignment as an equation
Ignoring time and state
Evaluate the current right side, then replace the target binding.
Use <= instead of < without checking equality
Missing the boundary partition
Test one value below, at, and above the threshold.
Assume division semantics transfer from another language
Using a remembered rule from C++
Use the explicitly stated Python operators; // floors toward negative infinity.

lessons.title: Loops and indexed collections
lessons.objective: Trace counted and condition-controlled loops, use valid zero-based list indices, and accumulate or filter values while accounting for empty inputs and termination.
scope: range stop excluded, nonzero signed step; zero iterations
while checks before body, update/termination; no execute-unbounded loop
Python lists as indexed collections, not claims of C++ array equivalence
Read/update positions, negative last index, len, out-of-range IndexError
Sum/count/filter list traversal, nested-loop counts
workedExamples: range(2,8,2) visits 2,4,6
A loop over range(0) leaves its initializer
Sum [3,-2,4] with a running total
Count values meeting an inclusive threshold
while doubles a value until crossing a bound
Identify a missing update that prevents termination
Read/replace first/last list positions and reject index len
Count iterations of two nested ranges

interaction.purpose: Choose a small list and threshold. Predict filtered sum and count, then step through every iteration with before/after state. Compare empty, all-rejected and boundary-equal inputs.

mistakes: Include range's stop
Confusing the boundary with a visited value
The stop is excluded even for negative steps.
Reset total inside the loop
Losing accumulated state
Initialize before traversal and update once per accepted item.
Treat len(items) as the last index
Counting positions from one
Nonnegative indices end at len(items)-1.
Assume a while loop runs once
Missing the initial condition check
The condition may be false before the first body execution.

lessons.title: Functions, contracts, and shared data
lessons.objective: Trace parameters, local variables and return values, distinguish printing from returning, and predict list aliasing versus a shallow copy under an explicit function contract.
scope: Function definition does not call it; parameters receive argument values
Return ends current call; no return yields None; print produces output and returns None
Local rebinding of immutable numeric argument does not rebind caller
Lists mutable, aliases share one object; items[:] shallow copy sufficient for flat numeric lists
Pure function vs mutation, preconditions/postconditions, nonempty mean versus empty case
workedExamples: Define scale(x,k) and trace two calls
A local x update leaves the caller's x unchanged
Trace an early return before later statements
A print-only function returns None
Function sum handles an empty list with zero
Mean requires a nonempty list; avoid zero division
Alias mutation changes the original list
A shallow copy isolates element replacement for a flat numeric list

interaction.purpose: Choose alias or shallow-copy behavior and an increment. Predict return and caller list values, then step through parameter binding, mutation and return with separate caller/callee state.

mistakes: Treat printed output as the return value
Confusing a side effect with an expression value
Only return supplies the call result; falling off returns None.
Assume parameter rebinding always changes the caller
Conflating names and objects
A new local binding does not replace the caller's binding.
Assume assigning a list copies its data
Missing aliasing
Both names reference the same list until explicitly copied or rebound.

lessons.title: Debugging with evidence and boundary tests
lessons.objective: Classify syntax, runtime and logic failures, trace the first divergent state, choose a justified repair, and design tests for normal, boundary and invalid cases without claiming that passing examples prove general correctness.
scope: Specification and expected result precede implementation
SyntaxError vs exception during execution vs wrong output without exception
Off-by-one range, wrong comparison, reset accumulator, premature return, empty mean
Choose smallest counterexample, inspect first wrong state, one hypothesis/change then regression checks
Exact integer assertions and stated tolerances for floats; no general floating equality claim
Input validity, empty/singleton/negative/duplicate/equality-boundary cases
workedExamples: Missing colon prevents parsing
Out-of-range access raises IndexError
Wrong comparison returns a plausible but incorrect answer
Repair sum range to include final element
Move accumulator initialization outside loop
Move return after traversal
Use empty/singleton/equality/negative regression cases
Compare computed 0.1+0.2 with 0.3 using a stated tolerance

interaction.purpose: Choose a faulty list-sum program and a proposed repair. Predict its output and whether it meets the specification, then reveal a trace and a small boundary-test matrix. Use a counterexample to reject a plausible repair.

mistakes: Change code before stating expected behavior
No comparison target
Write the contract and a failing example before proposing a repair.
Accept one passing case as proof
Insufficient input coverage
Keep tests across equivalence classes and boundaries; finite passing cases do not prove all inputs.
Use exact equality for approximate decimal computations
Ignoring binary representation
Compare absolute error with a justified tolerance.
